author: Joseph Lee
title: DOGE cuts cost tribes $470M, gutting funding for climate projects
content:
Every year, Kotzebue, a small city in northwest Alaska, has a three-month window to receive all the diesel fuel it will use throughout the following year. It sits on a gravel spit that juts into Kotzebue Sound just north of the Arctic Circle, and is accessible only by air and sea. Ice keeps freight barges from reaching it for most of the year.




The community relies on diesel for 75 percent of its power, and residents put about 20 percent of their income toward buying it. That’s more than three times the 

average energy burden

 for low-income households nationwide. 




“We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist. “Right now, with the Iran war going on, the diesel prices are very high and we’re locked in to much higher prices than we’ve had in the past. There’s really nothing the community can do about diesel prices, but what we can do is produce our own energy.”




That’s why Nordlum was so excited about a $20 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency to support a wind energy project. The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska. Nordlum says it would have lowered the community’s reliance on diesel to about 40 percent to 50 percent and given the tribe more control over energy and economic decisions. 




But the Trump administration canceled the grant in May 2025. More than a year later, the project remains paused. 




That cut was among hundreds of millions of dollars the Department of Government Efficiency pulled from Indian Country, and part of a broader pattern of funding rollbacks and 

underinvestment in Indigenous communities

. Two new reports from the Brookings Institution show that the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed many of the funding streams established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, while 

DOGE eliminated another $468 million

, about half of which was allocated for environmental and natural resources. Another 11 percent targeted agriculture. Those projects include climate resiliency plans, renewable energy projects, and jobs programs. 




According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues. Not only is that a violation of the 

federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to tribes

, it is hindering Indigenous efforts to protect the environment and address climate change. The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.




Rob Maxim, who is Mashpee Wampanoag and a fellow at Brookings Metro, said climate and environmental funding is especially crucial for Indigenous communities because they are often the most severely impacted by climate change, especially after years of underinvestment. 




“The actions that the Trump administration is taking are particularly significant, but it’s not totally out of trend with previous administrations,” he said. “And what we wanted to show was that actually this underinvestment is kind of the default for the U.S. rather than a blip.”




The true aberration was the unprecedented levels of funding after the pandemic. That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes. It covered projects like development of climate action plans, food systems analysis, and more. For example, the 

Hopi Tribe

 was to receive a $25 million grant to install solar panels for 600 homes. That grant, and the entire $7 billion Solar for All program, were cut. 




Kotzebue, Alaska, is accessible only by air and sea, and most of its fuel arrives in a three-month window before sea ice makes it difficult for ships to arrive.
 

Prisma Bildagentur / Universal Images Group via Getty Images




Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable. “The funding that was flowing to Indian Country was not being done on the basis of race or DEI, and it was absolutely not illegal,” he said. “It was aimed at the promotion of tribal sovereignty and the well-being of tribal citizens and tribal communities, and so that is, you know, an obligation that the U.S. government maintains.”




The White House and the EPA did respond to requests for comment. 




Glencora Haskins, a senior research associate and applied research manager at Brookings Metro, said that the administration had targeted funding to tribes, with “tribal” being 

the most frequently flagged term

. “I think that there was a very surface-level view of what a lot of these programs were doing, rather than any deep interrogation of the types of systemic infrastructure deficits that programs were trying to fix,” Haskins said. 




In Native communities throughout Alaska, and around the country, energy and infrastructure needs are especially acute because of increasingly frequent and destructive storms, wildfires, and other climate-driven disasters. 




Haskins and Maxim recommend that Congress pass legislation that bars the cancellation of grants and contracts for tribes, and stipulates that all funding for Indigenous nations and communities is in service of trust and treaty obligations even if it is from a program with a different stated purpose. They also call for a statutory requirement that money should flow directly to tribes rather than having them seek reimbursement from the U.S. Treasury.




In Kotzebue, Chad Nordlum hopes the political tide will turn enough to get the funding for the wind project moving. In the meantime, he is working on a smaller solar project that he hopes will help alleviate the community’s energy challenges.




“Our main goals are energy security and economic development for the tribe, which is ultimately being able to invest in our own community, help make the lives of people here a little more sustainable,” Nordlum said. “We want our community to continue on into the future. We have to get a handle on our energy prices and availability.”




This story was originally published by 

Grist

 with the headline 

DOGE cuts cost tribes $470M, gutting funding for climate projects

 on Nov 2, 2026.

author: Allison Herrera
title: Osage Nation speeds up orphan well cleanup as federal oversight recedes
content:
This story was originally published by

 

Osage News

, and is published through the Indigenous News Alliance.​




At the entrance to Harvest Land Farms, Fred Beartrack prepares to plug another orphaned well. Records indicated a cement plug covered it, but excavation and a casing cutout revealed no cement.




“There was no cement, so the data was wrong,” Beartrack of the Nation’s Department of Natural Resources, or DNR, said in a video posted to the Osage Nation’s Facebook page. The well was open down to 2,400 feet. Instead of a quick cap, the crew now has to clean the well out to the bottom and properly fill it with cement. Beartrack and his crew said this work could take anywhere from two days to two months.




“We don’t really know what’s down there,” he said. “People could have thrown anything in the well before we got here.”




Beartrack said crews found only about a foot of cement at the top of the well, with nothing beneath it. They drilled past the freshwater zone and cemented the well from there up.




“That well is an example of everything that’s wrong,” he said, referring to how the DNR has battled inaccurate well data as it has plugged wells throughout the Nation’s reservation, which covers about 1,470,559 acres in northeastern Oklahoma.




When Osage News spoke with Beartrack, the Department of Natural Resources was at the end of Phase 1 of the Nation’s federally funded orphan well program. Beartrack said the agency has plugged about 160 wells since the program began, 70 to 80 of them this year. Crews have inspected at least 2,500 to 2,700 wells.




“We keep finding new wells every quarter section we get into,” he said. Many go back decades, to operators that disappeared or wells that were plugged to standards now considered inadequate. The pace of well plugging picked up after a significant change this spring.




The Bureau of Indian Affairs’ Osage Agency used to approve every plugging permit the Nation filed. But on March 13, the Orphan Wells Plugging Office, or OWPO, revised its tribal grant guidelines for all Phase 1 and Phase 2 projects like the one Beartrack is working on.










Read Next




























How abandoned oil wells plague the Osage Nation













Naveena Sadasivam

,      

Lylla Younes

, &       

Allison Herrera

 



















The Bureau of Indian Affairs, or BIA, told the DNR that wells without a responsible party are not a federal function. That is a significant shift within the Osage Nation Reservation, where the BIA has long overseen oil and gas development as trustee of the Nation’s mineral estate, including drilling and plugging wells.




Adam Trumbly, superintendent for the Osage Agency in Pawhuska, said his office continues to review permits and issue well-plugging permits as appropriate. 




“The BIA–Osage Agency is not issuing plugging permits for orphan wells plugged pursuant to the Department of the Interior’s Orphaned Wells Program Office 

Tribal Orphaned Wells Program

,” Trumbly told Osage News in an email. “The Revised Tribal Grant Guidance removed the compliance requirements based on Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act.” 




Trumbly said this revision reflects OWPO’s determination that tribal development and tribal implementation grants are “nondiscretionary” and that activities conducted under them are not “federal undertakings.” 




He said this guidance means the Osage Nation no longer needs the BIA Osage Agency (or the Orphan Wells Plugging Office) to review orphan well plugging activities for Endangered Species Ace or National Historic Preservation Act compliance, and the BIA Osage Agency no longer has the authority to conduct those reviews.




The change follows 

a report

 that faulted the program’s slow start. Much of the blame stemmed from the Bureau’s lengthy permitting process. The criticism fits a longer pattern: Federal watchdogs have repeatedly faulted the BIA’s oversight of operators who work within the Osage Reservation.




Reporting by Grist and Osage News found roughly 2,300 documented orphaned wells in Osage, though the true number may be higher because many old wells were never recorded.  

Shane Brown / Grist / Osage News




Previously, the bureau reviewed each plugging application, verified the Department of Natural Resources’ photos and field data, then published a record of decision for a 30-day public comment period that often stretched to 45 days. Beartrack said the full process could take 120 to 130 days. Now, he said, it takes one to two weeks. The DNR still checks with the Osage Agency to confirm whether a well truly has no responsible party, whether leases were canceled or terminated, and how old they were.




“We ask the BIA almost daily questions,” Beartrack said.




The slowdown was a central theme of 

a February report

 from the Office of the Inspector General for the Interior Department. It found that as of December 31, 2024, the Osage Nation had plugged 14 of the 290 wells it planned for Phase 1, about 5 percent. The report cited delays in hiring a petroleum engineer, staffing shortages at the Osage Agency, and disagreements between the agency and the Nation over which permit applications qualified as emergencies.




As of January 30, the DNR had submitted 217 plugging permits since August of 2024. The Bureau of Indian Affairs had approved 90 of them. At a Natural Resources Committee meeting in March, Trumbly said the agency processed the permits as a courtesy and was working with a “skeleton crew” under a federal hiring freeze. Beartrack told Osage News that the agency had four or five people in the field to verify applications.




Adam Peltz, who works on orphan wells for the Environmental Defense Fund, or EDF, said tribal nations face hurdles that states don’t. Even if the Nation does the work well, it still needs the Bureau of Indian Affairs to review and approve its permits on time. “That part is out of Osage’s hands,” he said.




Peltz said the federal money itself is new. Until around 2020, he said, orphan wells were barely on the national radar. The bipartisan 

Regrow Act

, passed as part of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, set aside $4.7 billion for well plugging by states, federal agencies, and tribes. It was the first federal funding of its kind. About $150 million went to tribes, with the Osage Nation receiving the largest share.




When the EDF built a national orphan well map a few years ago, Peltz said there wasn’t any data available for Osage County. He said many tribal nations and the federal Bureau of Land Management never prioritized oversight of oil and gas, while some states have their own agencies and databases. State records on old wells aren’t much better, he added: Oklahoma has about 18,000 documented orphan wells and is believed to have more than 300,000 undocumented ones, said Peltz.




Beartrack said the Osage Agency didn’t hand the program over to the Nation so much as step away. “They just said wells without a responsible party are not a federal function,” he said. “It’s not like they gave us carte blanche. They just said it’s not their problem. They kind of wash their hands of it more than anything else.”










Read Next




























A new frontier in the voluntary carbon market: Old, leaky oil wells













Naveena Sadasivam

 



















That’s good for the program, he said, but it raises a bigger question for the Nation.




“What does that mean for the Osage Nation overall?” Beartrack said. “Are all of these orphan wells our responsibility? When they say that orphan wells are not a federal function, what does that mean?”




Beartrack said he believes Bureau of Indian Affairs leadership in Washington, D.C., made the decision, not the local agency. He said the bureau sent a formal letter announcing the change.




Former Principal Chief Geoffrey Standing Bear, now on the Osage Minerals Council, said he would like to see a scientific and environmental review for any federal action related to the change. The council has long argued that the BIA is the trustee of the Osage mineral estate.




The council focuses on attracting producers and leasing the mineral estate, while the Nation has kept the well plugging grant under the DNR. Peltz said the two goals shouldn’t conflict. Modern horizontal drilling in old fields only works if the old wells are plugged first, he said.




“Plugging old wells and developing new wells should not be in tension,” he said.







Before the change, much of the friction centered on what counted as an emergency. The Department of Natural Resources repeatedly flagged wells as emergencies; in March, Trumbly told committee members, “If everything’s an emergency, then nothing’s an emergency.”




Peltz said some states and tribes were filing almost nothing but emergency permits because it was the only way to break through the backlog. That isn’t how the system is supposed to work, he said. An emergency should be reserved for something like discovering a leaking well in someone’s backyard.




At the request of the Department of Natural Resources, the agency produced a weighted checklist. A score of 75 or higher for an actively leaking well or storage tank, high 

methane

 readings, or hydrogen sulfide near the wellhead marked a well as an emergency.




Beartrack said that the checklist never actually sped up permits. “It hasn’t changed any of the timing on how fast we get permits back,” he said.




A pumpjack in Osage County, where decades of oil and gas development have left the Osage Nation with a sprawling orphan-well cleanup.

 

Jim West / UCG / Universal Images Group via Getty Images




Peltz, who reviewed the checklist, said it closely resembles the scoring systems Texas and Louisiana use. An actively leaking well or storage tank threatens water and safety; high methane levels raise explosion risk; and hydrogen sulfide is among the most dangerous chemicals in the oil field. A measured fluid level above the deepest underground source of drinking water carries a weight of 50, below the threshold for an emergency. Peltz said that doesn’t prove groundwater is contaminated, but it is a risk factor worth checking.




“Could they have put that as a weight 75? Sure,” he said. “Is it a crime that they put it at 50? Not necessarily.”




The bigger problem, he said, is the scale. “The crime is that this was allowed to happen at this scale,” Peltz said, “and that it’s been so hard to work through it, even with the money flowing.”




The Department of Natural Resources still scores every well with it. Beartrack said some questions overlap or contradict each other. He has suggestions to fix them, but revising it isn’t a priority. “If it’s an emergency and the well has downhole conditions that would make it an emergency, then … we’re gonna plug it,” he said.




Beartrack said he is finishing contracts and purchase orders with rigs expected to roll in the next few weeks. Phase 2 has roughly 70 to 80 wells on deck to plug. He does not expect a dramatic jump in pace. “Maybe it should,” he said, “but … we’ll still be doing probably the same amount, 70 wells in this fiscal year.” The DNR’s field team is small, he said, and still has to gather and verify information for each well.




The Nation’s award comes to about $91 million over five years. Peltz said that won’t come close to covering Osage County, where no one knows how many orphan wells exist. Asked whether $91 million is enough, Peltz said, “No, not even close.” 




Previous reporting by Grist and Osage News found roughly 

2,300 documented orphaned wells in Osage

, though the true number may be higher because many old wells were never recorded. Plugging a single well costs anywhere from $40,000 to $500,000, depending on its condition.




Peltz said the program needs the Nation to hire more engineers and procurement staff to get bids out, “hopefully to Osage Nation contractors.” 




Asked whether oil drilling causes many of Osage County’s drinking water problems, Beartrack said, “Not if the wells are designed up to today’s standards.” That said, most of the wells his crews encounter are not. Many were drilled before operators routinely set surface casing deep enough to protect fresh water — something Beartrack said didn’t take hold until around the 1970s. Older wells, he said, “were OK for the standard of the day.”




At Harvest Land, the crew planned to finish the job the same way at every site: Clear the land, remediate it, and return it to its original surface, with the well capped and buried. “The final result is you won’t see anything,” Beartrack said. “And we’ll have a record of where it was.”




This story was originally published by 

Grist

 with the headline 

Osage Nation speeds up orphan well cleanup as federal oversight recedes

 on Nov 2, 2026.

author: Joseph Lee
title: For Indigenous peoples in Brazil, the election results offer a reprieve — not a resolution
content:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection as president of Brazil gave Indigenous communities a measure of relief after a campaign in which his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, promised to halt recognition of new Indigenous territories and push for more mining and development.




“For Indigenous Peoples, the reelection of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is more than a victory, and it is bigger than Brazil,” said Edson Krenak, who is Indigenous Krenak. “It is not about victory; it is about the possibility to dream and to fight without fear of death.”




But Sunday’s runoff election strengthened Bolsonaro’s movement in Congress, where his Liberal Party won the largest number of seats in both houses and the broader right gained a Senate majority. Leaders warn that this could open their territories to mining, weaken environmental protections, and roll back land rights, making it much harder for Lula to advance his Indigenous and environmental agendas.




Climate Observatory, a nonprofit coalition of 172 organizations, says 

70 percent of the incoming lawmakers

 oppose the climate and environmental agenda, according to The Associated Press.




The stakes were especially high for Indigenous peoples because Bolsonaro campaigned on policies aligned with those of his father Jair Bolsonaro, whose presidency from 2019 to 2023 saw an increase in mining, land grabs, 

deforestation

, and 

attacks on their rights

. Amazon deforestation reached a record in 2022, and Indigenous leaders say their communities endured unchecked violence from illegal mining operations during the elder Bolsonaro’s time in office.




His son finished more than 2 million votes ahead of Lula in the first election earlier this month, but neither candidate secured the 50 percent required to win outright. That result sparked fear in Indigenous communities and environmental advocates, who warned that 

the future of the Amazon was at stake

. Lula came back to win Sunday’s runoff by roughly 4.4 million votes, securing a fourth, nonconsecutive term as president.




In an interview between the two rounds of voting, Toya Manchineri, the general coordinator of the Coordination of Indigenous Organizations of the Brazilian Amazon, or COIAB, said Indigenous peoples across the rainforest were deeply concerned about the possibility of a Bolsonaro win. Much of the last three years of Lula’s administration were spent undoing the damage the Bolsonaro administration caused, Manchineri said.




Manchineri said Lula’s term has largely been a period of rebuilding as Indigenous peoples gained greater roles in decision making. “We were only beginning to see the resources returning,” he said.




In 2023, the administration established the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples and appointed Sônia Guajajara to lead it. Lula also revitalized the federal Indigenous affairs agency FUNAI after Bolsonaro had used it to support agribusiness, despite Indigenous resistance. The government also announced just before the election that Amazon 

deforestation had fallen to its lowest level

 since recordkeeping began in 1988, according to the AP.




Still, Indigenous leaders say the progress made under Lula has not resolved deeper conflicts over land, development, and decision-making.




“Lula’s victory prevents a president who promised to halt Indigenous land demarcation from taking office, but our territories are far from safe,” Alessandra Korap Munduruku, coordinator of the Munduruku Pariri Indigenous Association, 

said in a statement

. “We have demanded that Lula’s government respect our decisions and listen to Indigenous Peoples before advancing projects that affect our rivers and forests. Congress has become more dangerous for us, and we must remain organized. Our struggle does not end with an election’s outcome.” 




For Indigenous organizations, Lula’s victory is cause for hope, but they must now work with a Congress dominated by lawmakers who have already voted in favor of easing environmental protections and against Indigenous land claims. Given that dynamic, Krenak expressed concern about the difficulty Lula may face advancing his agenda. “The costs of negotiating with the Congress and senate will be very high, if ever successful,” he said.




The election also came amid years of Indigenous voters struggling to access the polls. Earlier this month, a court denied a request for transportation assistance filed by Indigenous peoples in the Javari Valley in northern Brazil. Other efforts were more successful: Court rulings elsewhere helped 

secure government transportation

 for Indigenous voters in remote areas, while Indigenous communities across the Amazon organized to increase turnout, AP reported.




“Despite the challenges faced throughout the electoral process, Indigenous peoples of the Amazon made their voices heard at the polls across all nine states of the Brazilian Amazon, reaffirming their commitment to democracy, national sovereignty, and the defense of Indigenous rights. We marked the ballot boxes in defense of life, our territories, and Brazil’s future!” COIAB said in a statement. “Brazil’s future is Indigenous, and it begins in our territories! WE ARE THE ANSWER!”




For Krenak, however, Lula’s victory is only the beginning. He says he wants to see more meaningful progress during the president’s next term.




“By 2030, success should not be measured by how many Indigenous leaders stand besides officials at summits,” he said. “But by whether Indigenous Peoples gain real authority to prevent their territories to become sacrifice zones, but territories of life, reciprocity and generosity.”




This story was originally published by 

Grist

 with the headline 

For Indigenous peoples in Brazil, the election results offer a reprieve — not a resolution

 on Oct 28, 2026.

author: Vivian La
title: In Michigan, 3 tribes are on a mission to bring back a fish that disappeared 100 years ago
content:
Even when they’re young, the characteristic iridescent hues of the Arctic grayling are noticeable at the right angle.




On a brisk morning in September, fish and wildlife biologist Sean Leask counted and measured hundreds of these fish, which were raised at the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians’ streamside rearing facility, located just outside Traverse City in northern Michigan. 




“Some of these might be catchable by the end of next year,” Leask said. “I don’t know what their growth will look like in the wild.”




That’s because Arctic grayling haven’t been seen in Michigan waters for almost a century. By the 1930s, industrial activity like logging and overfishing, along with competition from non-native fish, had decimated their numbers. But three northern Michigan tribes and the state are trying to change that by reintroducing the fish to local waters. 




“Our taking care of them and helping them to reestablish their population helps us to reestablish ourselves, our culture, and our traditions,” said Tina Frankenberger, the Grand Traverse Band’s tribal environmental resiliency lead.




Their work joins broader efforts by tribes around the country to restore native species — from 

salmon

 to 

oysters

 to 

condors

 — that are culturally and economically important, while also strengthening the ecosystems that these species depend on against threat

author: Joseph Lee
title: Long after the Maui fires, toxic metals linger in residents’ bodies
content:
In August of 2023, a series of wildfires broke out across Maui, killing more than 100 people, destroying thousands of homes, and causing billions in damage. Noelani Ahia, who is Kanaka Maoli and co-founder of Maui Medic Healers Hui, helped mobilize nearly 600 volunteers in Lāhainā, including doctors, nurses, and therapists. 




Three years later, the housing and health crises remain acute. Maui Medic Healers Hui runs a free clinic, but Ahia wishes it had 10 more to address the community’s needs. “The fire may be out, but the catastrophe is not over by any stretch of the imagination,” she said. 




The devastation extended well beyond the lives lost and buildings destroyed. Research published last year by researchers with the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, found that 

more than 1 in 5 residents

 had reduced lung function.




Now, new research from the same project has 

found elevated levels of toxic metals

 in the island’s residents months after the fires, with higher exposure associated with impaired lung function. The findings offer further evidence that 

the health consequences of catastrophic wildfires

 can persist long after the flames are extinguished and the smoke clears.

author: Michael Beltran
title: America’s AI ambitions threaten Indigenous lands in the Philippines
content:
This is an original story by 

Mongabay

 republished through the Indigenous News Alliance.




Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. arrived at the Grand Hyatt Manila on Sept. 10 to address hundreds of foreign business representatives assembled for the Luzon Economic Corridor investors’ forum.




Outside the hotel, hundreds of demonstrators had also gathered, carrying signs that read “No to Pax Silica!” The scene reflected both the government’s ambitious plans to ride the artificial intelligence wave and deep ambivalence in civil society.




Police confronted the crowd, shoving them with riot shields and batons on the street outside the hotel lobby. Activists say police injured at least 27 protesters and arrested five. Police, meanwhile, reported minor cuts and injuries to 16 personnel. 




Protester Jona Yang, from the activist-scientist group AGHAM, said she was negotiating with the police to cool tensions when they arrested her. “We want the Marcos government and investors to see the outrage all of this has caused,” Yang told Mongabay. “They’re taking away our resources and our lands.”




The Luzon Economic Corridor, or LEC, is an economic initiative focused on the Philippines’ biggest island, begun in 2024. Pax Silica, the U.S.-led global pact to build an AI and semiconductor supply chain that is not reliant on China, includes the LEC. In April, Washington and Mani

author: Austin Corona
title: The bipartisan energy bill tearing the climate movement apart
content:
In order to solve climate change, you have to do two things — stop burning fossil fuels, and build clean energy to replace them. The last few decades in the United States have witnessed a long back-and-forth over which of the two goals is more important, and over how to achieve either of them. Is it more important to pass a carbon tax, or subsidize electric vehicles? To block a new oil pipeline, or build a lot of solar and wind? 




On this question, the coalition known as the climate movement has fractured into two broad groups. On one side, there are activists, lawyers, and environmentalists, who tend to focus on blocking and reducing fossil fuel use. On the other, there are renewable energy companies and policy wonks, who tend to focus on building more clean energy.




These factions have clashed in the past, but over the past week a kind of civil war has erupted between the different elements of the climate movement. The inciting incident was the release of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, a long-awaited Senate bill that is designed to enable the construction of more power plants, transmission lines, and gas pipelines. The bill does this by weakening some of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws, speeding up the timeline for government agencies to issue permits, and making it harder to cancel projects that have already gotten federal approva
